title: Mars Had a Mega-Flood! This Giant Valley Is the Proof
summary:
Imagine a flood so big it could carve a valley as long as the whole country of Italy! That's what happened on Mars billions of years ago, and we have the pictures to prove it. A spacecraft called Mars Express has been snapping amazing photos of Shalbatana Vallis, a gigantic valley near Mars's equator. It stretches 1,300 kilometers and is up to 10 kilometers wide and 500 meters deep — that's like stacking three Washington Monuments on top of each other!

Scientists think this valley formed about 3.5 billion years ago when a huge amount of underground water burst onto the surface. The water rushed downhill, ripping through the landscape and carving deep channels. Over time, the valley partly filled up with stuff — you can even see a dark patch that's probably volcanic ash blown around by Martian winds.

But here's the coolest part: this valley is one of many that empty into a low, flat area called Chryse Planitia. Because so many water channels end there, some scientists believe this area might have held a big ocean long ago, when Mars was warmer and wetter. The pictures also show "chaotic terrain" — jumbled blocks of rock that formed when underground ice melted and the ground collapsed, like a sinkhole. There are also old lava flows, impact craters, and flat-topped hills called mesas.

Mars Express has been orbiting the Red Planet for over 20 years, mapping everything in 3D. These new images help us piece together the story of water on Mars — and maybe, just maybe, whether it could have been a home for life.
why_it_matters: Learning about water on Mars helps you imagine if someday humans could visit or even live there, sparking dreams of becoming an astronaut or scientist.

background_read: Today Mars is a cold, dry desert, but billions of years ago it was warmer and wetter, with rivers and maybe even large lakes or oceans.
Shalbatana Vallis is one of many huge outflow channels on Mars that suggest sudden, enormous floods happened when underground water burst onto the surface.
Chryse Planitia (a broad lowland on Mars) is where several of these channels meet, leading scientists to think water once pooled there like a big sea.
Mars Express (a European Space Agency orbiter launched in 2003) has mapped almost the whole planet in 3D, helping us piece together Mars's watery past.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists studying photos from Mars Express
WHAT: Found evidence that a mega-flood carved Shalbatana Vallis billions of years ago
WHERE: Near Mars's equator, a valley 1,300 km long and up to 10 km wide
WHY: The images show features like chaotic terrain, old lava flows, and channels that point to sudden release of underground water, helping us understand if Mars could have ever supported life.

perspectives.description: They see this as one more strong piece of evidence that Mars had liquid water on its surface, raising hope that ancient life might have existed there.
Some argue that lava flows or glaciers could also explain some features, so we need more clues like minerals that only form in water to be completely sure.
They look at these flood channels as a sign that underground water might still be trapped beneath Mars’s surface, a possible resource for future astronauts.
